questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman attended for review after a positive pregnancy test. She was known to have HIV and was taking tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine/efavirenz. She reported ongoing compliance with her medication. She estimated that she was 7 weeks pregnant. Investigations: CD4 count 550 cells/μL HIV viral load undetectable
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Advise her to consider termination due to the risk of teratogenicity
Continue current ART and routine monitoring
Stop ART and recommence during the 2nd trimester
Switch to ritonavir-boosted darunavir, zidovudine, and emtricitabine

questions.explanation: Continue current ART and routine monitoring HIV-infected pregnant women established on ART who present for care during the 1st trimester should continue treatment during pregnancy, provided the regimen is tolerated and effective in suppressing viral replication. Women who become pregnant on efavirenz-containing regimens who are virally suppressed and tolerating it should continue their current regimens. In the past efavirenz was linked with teratogenicity based on animal studies; however, increased teratogenicity has not been seen in the babies of mothers exposed to efavirenz in the 1st trimester in registry studies and meta-analyses. Therefore guidelines recommend continuing treatment: http://aidsinfo.nih.gov/contentfiles/lvgu idelines/PerinatalGL.pd. There is no data on cobicistat in pregnancy, therefore for present protease inhibitors should be ritonavir-boosted.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q34

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman, a refugee from sub-Saharan Africa who recently moved to Canada, is 36 weeks pregnant. Her screening HIV test is positive, viral load is 77,000 copies/mL and CD4 count is 210 cells/mm3. She is otherwise healthy and genotype and HLA-B*5701 testing are awaited.
questions.question_raw: 34yo F, refugee from SS Africa, recently moved to Canada and is 36 weeks pregnant. Screening HIV test positive. Viral load is 77,000 copies/mL, CD4 count is 210. Otherwise healthy. Awaiting genotype and HLAB5701 testing.

parts.text: Give three appropriate antiretroviral regimens and when you would start each.
Give the regimen for intrapartum antiretroviral therapy and the mode of delivery.
The mother's viral load at the time of delivery is 2700 copies/mL. What is your regimen for the baby and what is the duration of each component?
What is one test you need to do in the immediate postpartum period, and give the timing.
What is your advice regarding breastfeeding, and give two reasons.

parts_raw.text: Give three appropriate ART regimens and when you would start each
Give the regimen for intrapartum ART therapy and mode of delivery
VL of mother at time of delivery is 2700 copies/mL. What is your regimen for the baby and what is the duration of each component.
What is ONE test you need to do in immediate post-partum period and give timing
What is your advice regarding breastfeeding and give TWO reasons

questions.model_answer:
a) Start ART immediately, at diagnosis, regardless of gestational age, CD4 count or viral load - do not wait for the genotype or HLA-B*5701 result; resistance testing is recommended before initiating therapy in pregnancy but treatment is started empirically and adjusted when it returns. Three appropriate regimens: (1) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine plus dolutegravir 50 mg daily. (2) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine plus raltegravir 400 mg twice daily. (3) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine plus ritonavir-boosted darunavir 600/100 mg twice daily (or boosted atazanavir). Abacavir/lamivudine may replace the tenofovir backbone once HLA-B*5701 is negative. Efavirenz is avoided at conception/first trimester because of neural tube defects, and dolutegravir requires counselling about a possible first-trimester neural tube defect risk. At 36 weeks all three are started today - there is no role for deferral, since every week of viraemia adds transmission risk.

b) Continue the oral regimen through labour and add intravenous zidovudine, 2 mg/kg loading dose over 1 hour then 1 mg/kg/h until the cord is clamped, because the viral load is >1000 copies/mL. Recommend scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks' gestation for a viral load >1000 copies/mL near delivery.

c) Maternal viral load 2700 copies/mL means high-risk exposure: give presumptive three-drug neonatal therapy started within 6 hours of birth - zidovudine for 6 weeks, lamivudine for 6 weeks, and nevirapine (treatment dose) for the first 2-6 weeks. A commonly used Canadian alternative is zidovudine for 6 weeks plus three doses of nevirapine in the first week.

d) HIV virologic testing by nucleic acid amplification (HIV DNA/RNA PCR), not serology, because maternal antibody persists. For a high-risk infant test within the first 48 hours of life, then at 14-21 days, 1-2 months and 4-6 months.

e) Advise against breastfeeding and support exclusive formula feeding. (1) HIV is transmitted in breast milk and the residual risk persists even with maternal ART and viral suppression. (2) In Canada, replacement feeding is acceptable, feasible, affordable, sustainable and safe, so the risk is avoidable.
questions.beyond_mandell: Perinatal specifics (pregnancy regimen choice, intrapartum IV zidovudine threshold, cesarean at 38 weeks, neonatal prophylaxis, infant NAAT timing, feeding advice) follow the HHS Perinatal HIV guidelines and Canadian (CPS) guidance.

questions.question: A woman with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection is 16 weeks pregnant, with viral load 77,000 copies/mL and CD4 210 cells/mm3. HLA-B*5701 and resistance testing are pending.
questions.question_raw: HIV in Pregnancy at 16 weeks gestation. VL 77K, CD4 210. HLA and resistance testing is pending.

parts.text: Name three first-line agents to start, and when.
What should be given peripartum (viral load is 2100 copies/mL)?
What is your recommended delivery method?
What HIV diagnostic test is required for the neonate, and how soon?
How do you treat the baby, and for how long?
What is your recommendation for infant feeding, and two reasons why?

parts_raw.text: Name 3 first line agents to start, and when?
What to give peripartum (VL is 2100)
What is your recommended delivery method?
What HIV diagnostic test is required for the neonate and how soon?
How do you treat the baby and for how long
What is your recommendation for infant feeding and 2 reasons why

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Dolutegravir 50 mg once daily. (2) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg once daily. (3) Emtricitabine 200 mg once daily. Start immediately — pregnancy favours early initiation and therapy should not be delayed for pending results; abacavir is excluded until HLA-B*5701 is known, and at 16 weeks she is beyond the periconception neural-tube-defect window of concern for dolutegravir.
b) Intravenous zidovudine in labour: 2 mg/kg loading dose over 1 hour, then 1 mg/kg/h until the cord is clamped (viral load >1000 copies/mL), continuing her oral combination ART.
c) Scheduled pre-labour caesarean section at 38 weeks, because the viral load exceeds 1000 copies/mL near delivery.
d) HIV DNA/RNA nucleic acid amplification test (virologic test, not serology) — first within 48 hours of birth, repeated at 2-3 weeks (or 1-2 months) and 4-6 months.
e) High-risk presumptive therapy: zidovudine plus lamivudine plus nevirapine (or raltegravir) for 6 weeks.
f) Avoid breastfeeding; formula feed exclusively. (1) Breast milk transmits HIV and the risk is not eliminated by maternal ART, particularly with detectable viraemia. (2) Safe, affordable, sustainable replacement feeding is available in Canada, so formula carries no offsetting mortality risk.
questions.beyond_mandell: Perinatal HIV (DHHS/Canadian) guidelines supply the peripartum IV zidovudine and caesarean threshold (VL >1000), infant NAT schedule, 6-week high-risk infant prophylaxis, and the Canadian recommendation against breastfeeding.

questions.question: A pregnant woman from Africa is newly diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection at 36 weeks gestation. Viral load is 78,000 copies/mL; resistance testing and HLA-B*5701 are pending.
questions.question_raw: New diagnosis HIV in pregnant woman from Africa at 36 weeks gestation. Viral load 78k, resistance testing and HLA-B*5701 pending.

parts.text: What are three antiretroviral regimens to start, and when would you start each?
She has a stat viral load at delivery showing 2700 copies/mL. What management do you recommend for her delivery?
The baby is born. What regimen do you prescribe for the baby, and for how long?
What is Canada's recommendation regarding infant feeding? Give two reasons why.

parts_raw.text: What are three art regimens to start, and when would you start each?
She has a stat viral load at delivery showing viral load 2700. What management do you recommend for her delivery?
The baby is born. What regimen do you prescribe for baby and for how long?
What is Canada’s recommendation regarding infant feeding? Give two reasons why.

questions.model_answer:
a) Start immediately — today, without waiting for pending results (pregnancy favours early initiation and time to delivery is short; rapid same-day initiation is feasible and beneficial). (1) Dolutegravir 50 mg daily plus tenofovir (TDF or TAF)-emtricitabine — preferred for the most rapid viral decay. (2) Raltegravir 400 mg twice daily plus tenofovir-emtricitabine. (3) Ritonavir-boosted darunavir or atazanavir plus tenofovir-emtricitabine (note the possible increased preterm delivery risk with PI-based ART). Abacavir-lamivudine only once HLA-B*5701 is negative, and it should be used with caution when viral load exceeds 100,000 copies/mL.
b) Viral load >1000 copies/mL: scheduled pre-labour caesarean section plus intravenous zidovudine, 2 mg/kg loading dose over 1 hour then 1 mg/kg/h until the umbilical cord is clamped, with her oral ART continued.
c) Presumptive high-risk therapy: zidovudine plus lamivudine plus nevirapine (or raltegravir) for 6 weeks, starting within 6 hours of birth.
d) Do not breastfeed; formula feed exclusively. (1) Breast milk transmits HIV and the risk persists even on maternal ART, especially with detectable viraemia as here. (2) Safe, clean, affordable replacement feeding is reliably available in Canada, so avoiding breastfeeding carries no competing infectious or nutritional risk.
questions.beyond_mandell: Perinatal HIV (DHHS/Canadian) guidelines supply the caesarean threshold of VL >1000, IV zidovudine in labour, the 6-week high-risk infant regimen, and the Canadian recommendation against breastfeeding.

questions.question: A 38-week pregnant, otherwise healthy woman has been on Biktarvy for her entire pregnancy and is virologically suppressed. She is interested in breastfeeding.
questions.question_raw: You have a mother in clinic who is 38-weeks pregnant who is otherwise healthy. She has been on Biktarvy for her entire pregnancy and is virologically suppressed. She is interested in breastfeeding.

parts.text: Based on the Canadian Pediatric & Perinatal HIV/AIDS Research Group consensus recommendations for infant feeding in HIV, what are three criteria to proceed with breastfeeding?

parts_raw.text: Based on the Canadian Pediatric & Perinatal HIV/AIDS Research group consensus recommendations for infant feeding in HIV, what are THREE criteria to proceed with breast feeding?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) The parent is on ART with sustained virologic suppression (HIV RNA undetectable) from before/through pregnancy and commits to continuing ART with ongoing suppression through the breastfeeding period. (2) Engagement in care with a commitment to enhanced maternal and infant monitoring - frequent maternal viral loads (about monthly) and infant HIV testing during and after breastfeeding. (3) Exclusive breastfeeding (no mixed feeding) for a defined limited duration, with prompt attention to mastitis/cracked nipples or infant gastrointestinal illness and a plan to stop if viremia occurs; the decision is informed, shared, and non-coercive.
questions.beyond_mandell: Canadian Pediatric & Perinatal HIV/AIDS Research Group consensus statement on infant feeding in the context of HIV (2023); not covered in this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: A woman with HIV presents in labour having received no antenatal care.
questions.question_raw: HIV+ mom presents at delivery with no antenatal care

parts.text: What is the baby's risk of acquiring HIV?

parts_raw.text: What is baby's risk of acquiring HIV?

questions.model_answer: a) Approximately 13% to 39% (commonly quoted 25%) without any antepartum or intrapartum antiretroviral therapy; with a full antenatal/intrapartum/neonatal regimen the rate falls to under 2%.

cohort_answer.text: 25-40% without ARVs; 1-2% with ARVs

questions.question: A woman with HIV presents in labour having received no antenatal care.
questions.question_raw: HIV+ mom presents at delivery with no antenatal care

parts.text: List four (or seven) factors that increase the risk of mother-to-child transmission.

parts_raw.text: List 4 (or 7) factors that increase the risk

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Absent or late-initiated combination ART during pregnancy (no antepartum/intrapartum drugs, or start only in late second/third trimester). (2) Maternal HIV RNA >1000 copies/mL (any detectable viral load) near delivery. (3) Low maternal CD4+ T-cell count. (4) Acute/primary HIV infection or seroconversion during pregnancy or breastfeeding. (5) Prolonged rupture of membranes. (6) Preterm delivery. (7) Concomitant genital ulcerative disease; vaginal delivery without viral suppression and breastfeeding are additional risks.

cohort_answer.text: Considered HIGH RISK for transmission: Mother has acute or early untreated infection; Mother with viral load >1000 copies/mL within 4 weeks of delivery; Mother received no ART or less than 4 weeks of ART by time of delivery; little/no prenatal care especially at risk; Maternal immunologic status/WHO clinical stage (increased risk with CD4<200); Premature birth; Vaginal delivery among mothers with VL>1000; Heavy bleeding during delivery among those with detectable VL; Chorioamnionitis; Maternal mastitis

questions.question: A woman with HIV presents in labour having received no antenatal care.
questions.question_raw: HIV+ mom presents at delivery with no antenatal care

parts.text: What do you do for the baby?

parts_raw.text: What do you do for baby?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Delivery measures: cesarean section if viral load is not suppressed (<1000 copies/mL) and before rupture of membranes; avoid fetal scalp electrodes and forceps/vacuum. (2) Antiretrovirals as soon as possible, preferably within 6-12 hours of life: this is a higher-risk/presumed-exposure infant, so give combination prophylaxis (6 weeks zidovudine plus three doses of nevirapine at birth, 48 h, and 96 h later) or, preferred, empirical HIV therapy with 6 weeks of zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine or zidovudine + lamivudine + raltegravir. (3) Contraindicate breastfeeding in a resource-rich setting; standard precautions, then routine bathing, vitamin K, and eye prophylaxis. (4) Diagnostic HIV nucleic acid tests at 14-21 days, 1-2 months, and 4-6 months, with an additional test in the first 48 hours in this high-risk infant and one 2-4 weeks after stopping antiretrovirals (8-10 weeks). (5) Offer HIV testing to the mother and her other children.
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS perinatal HIV guidelines: also give intrapartum IV zidovudine to the mother and send a stat maternal HIV viral load.

cohort_answer.text: At delivery: C/S prior to onset of rupture of membranes recommended; Intrapartum IV zidovudine; Avoidance of fetal scalp electrode monitoring; STAT HIV VL. Interventions on infant: LOW RISK: monotherapy PEP (4 weeks) with zidovudine; HIGH RISK: combination PEP (6 weeks) - 2 drug regimen AZT+3 doses NVP (resource-limited) or 3 drug regimen AZT, 3TC, treatment dose NVP (preferred). Advise against breastfeeding (developed countries). Test baby for HIV PCR at birth, 2 weeks, 1, 2, 4, 18 months

questions.question: A woman with HIV presents in labour having received no antenatal care; the baby tests HIV positive by PCR.
questions.question_raw: HIV+ mom presents at delivery with no antenatal care. Baby tests HIV+ by PCR.

parts.text: What do you do now?

parts_raw.text: Now what?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Confirm the diagnosis immediately with a second nucleic acid test, either the same assay on a new sample or the alternative assay (RNA if DNA PCR was used, or vice versa) on the original sample. (2) Convert to HIV therapy: combination ART with zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine at treatment doses, or zidovudine + lamivudine + raltegravir, given lifelong. (3) Refer to a pediatric HIV specialist; test the mother's other children regardless of age.
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS pediatric OI guidelines: start trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole PJP prophylaxis from 4-6 weeks through 12 months of age regardless of CD4 count.

cohort_answer.text: Confirm HIV infection: positive PCR x2 prior to 18 months or reactive serology after 18 months. Continue 3-drug treatment regimen: Two NRTIs (AZT+3TC) + NVP, or Two NRTIs (AZT+3TC) + RAL (weight>2kg). Prevent opportunistic infection: start co-trimoxazole in infants (1st year of life) regardless of CD4 count (high risk PJP). Referral to pediatric HIV care provider

questions.question: A pregnant woman with HIV has a CD4 count of 550 and viral load of 20,000 copies/mL and does not want treatment for herself.
questions.question_raw: Pregnant woman with CD4 550 and VL 20,000. Doesn't want treatment for herself.

parts.text: What three things can be done to decrease the risk of transmission to the baby?

parts_raw.text: What 3 things can be done to decrease the risk of transmission to baby?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Scheduled cesarean delivery before rupture of membranes, since viral load is not suppressed below 1000 copies/mL (with avoidance of fetal scalp electrodes and operative vaginal delivery). (2) Neonatal antiretrovirals begun within 6-12 hours of birth - combination prophylaxis or empirical therapy given the unsuppressed maternal viral load. (3) Complete avoidance of breastfeeding.
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS perinatal guidelines: intrapartum IV zidovudine is also indicated when viral load exceeds 1000 copies/mL.

cohort_answer.text: C-section; Intra-partum prophylaxis with IV zidovudine; Post-partum prophylaxis; Avoid breastfeeding for the infant with zidovudine x6 weeks +/- nevirapine x1 week depending on maternal VL; Washing infant prior to Vitamin K injection

questions.question: A pregnant woman with HIV declines treatment for herself.
questions.question_raw: Pregnant HIV+ woman declines treatment for herself.

parts.text: What three recommendations can you make to the obstetrician to decrease the risk of transmission to the baby?

parts_raw.text: What 3 recommendations can you make to the OBGYN to decrease the risk of transmission to baby?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Perform a scheduled cesarean section before rupture of membranes because viral suppression below 1000 copies/mL has not been achieved. (2) Avoid fetal scalp electrodes for monitoring and avoid forceps or vacuum extraction; avoid artificial rupture of membranes and prolonged membrane rupture. (3) Counsel against breastfeeding.

cohort_answer.text: C/S prior to rupture of membranes; Clean baby well prior to admin of vitamin K; Avoid artificial rupture of membranes; Avoid operative delivery with forceps or vacuum extractor; Avoid fetal scalp electrodes; Avoid breastfeeding

questions.question: A pregnant woman with HIV is untreated (CD4 550, viral load 1000 copies/mL) and is expecting her second child; she took combination antiretroviral therapy during her first pregnancy and that daughter was uninfected. She does not want treatment for herself at this time.
questions.question_raw: HIV in pregnancy: MTCT. A pregnant woman HIV+ who is not currently treated (CD4 550, VL 1000) is having her second child. She took HAART during her first pregnancy and had a seronegative daughter. She does not want treatment for herself at this time.

parts.text: Suggest the optimal pre-partum regimen.
When would you treat?

parts_raw.text: Suggest optimal pre-partum regimen
When would you treat?

questions.model_answer:
a) Antenatal combination ART for the mother is the single most effective intervention and should be strongly recommended (a two-NRTI backbone plus an integrase inhibitor); if she still declines, the fallback is intrapartum antiretroviral coverage plus scheduled cesarean before rupture of membranes and combination neonatal prophylaxis, recognizing that interventions begun at delivery do not prevent in-utero infection.
b) Now - treat throughout pregnancy, as early as possible. ART started before conception gives an MTCT rate of 0.2% versus 1.1% when started during pregnancy, and no transmissions occurred among women on ART from before conception with <50 copies/mL at delivery; delayed or absent ART is a leading correlate of transmission. She also meets criteria for lifelong therapy for her own health.
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS perinatal guidelines: preferred antenatal regimen is tenofovir/emtricitabine (or abacavir/lamivudine) with dolutegravir, plus intrapartum IV zidovudine if viral load is >1000 or unknown.

cohort_answer.text: Intra-partum IV zidovudine during labor until delivery; Schedule C-section before rupture of membranes; Infant post-partum prophylaxis

questions.question: A woman with HIV presents at 34 weeks of pregnancy.
questions.question_raw: HIV+ woman at 34 weeks pregnancy

parts.text: Outline your management.

parts_raw.text: Management

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Start combination ART immediately for maternal health and to prevent antenatal and intrapartum transmission; check viral load and CD4 count, resistance testing, and screen for co-infections. (2) Plan delivery on viral load: scheduled cesarean before rupture of membranes if HIV RNA is not <1000 copies/mL at ~36 weeks; avoid fetal scalp electrodes and operative vaginal delivery. (3) Counsel against breastfeeding. (4) Neonatal antiretrovirals within 6-12 hours of birth - because ART was started only in the third trimester the infant is higher risk and needs combination prophylaxis or empirical therapy - with nucleic acid testing at 14-21 days, 1-2 months, and 4-6 months. (5) Offer HIV testing to her other children.
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS perinatal guidelines: add intrapartum IV zidovudine when viral load is >1000 copies/mL or unknown.

cohort_answer.text: Does she want treatment? Yes: Start ART right away with INSTI based regimen if able, IV zidovudine during labour. No: IV zidovudine during labour

questions.question: A woman with HIV presents at 34 weeks of pregnancy.
questions.question_raw: HIV+ woman at 34 weeks pregnancy

parts.text: Can she have a vaginal delivery?

parts_raw.text: Can she have a vaginal delivery?

questions.model_answer: a) Yes, if she is on combination ART and has achieved viral suppression below 1000 copies/mL near delivery; if suppression has not been achieved (or viral load is unknown), scheduled cesarean section before labour and before rupture of membranes is recommended.

cohort_answer.text: Depends on whether she is on ART and if VL<1000 copies. Ideally scheduled C/S at 38 weeks (if VL>1000, definitely needs C/S) prior to rupture of membranes

questions.question: A woman is found to be HIV positive at 16 weeks of gestation, with a viral load of 16,000 copies/mL and CD4 count of 410.
questions.question_raw: A mother is found to be HIV+ at 16 weeks gestation. VL 16,000 copies/mL and CD4 410.

parts.text: Would you treat her?

parts_raw.text: Would you treat her?

questions.model_answer: a) Yes - start combination ART immediately, for her own health and because antenatal ART is the single most effective means of preventing mother-to-child transmission.

cohort_answer.text: Yes

questions.question: A woman is found to be HIV positive at 16 weeks of gestation, with a viral load of 16,000 copies/mL and CD4 count of 410.
questions.question_raw: A mother is found to be HIV+ at 16 weeks gestation. VL 16,000 copies/mL and CD4 410.

parts.text: If so, what medications would you use, and give your rationale.

parts_raw.text: If so, what meds and give your rationale?

questions.model_answer: a) A three-drug combination regimen: a two-NRTI backbone (tenofovir/emtricitabine or abacavir/lamivudine) plus an integrase inhibitor. Rationale: without antepartum or intrapartum ART the transmission rate is 13-39%; the antenatal-intrapartum-neonatal regimen dropped US transmission from 25% to 8% and current rates are under 2%, and women on ART from before conception with viral load <50 copies/mL at delivery had no transmissions. Suppression to <1000 copies/mL by delivery also avoids the need for cesarean section.
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS perinatal guidelines supply the specific preferred regimens (e.g. tenofovir/emtricitabine plus dolutegravir); Mandell defers regimen choice to Chapter 126.

cohort_answer.text: Refer to previous slide for regimen options (easiest to remember: Truvada and dolutegravir). Rationale: risk of vertical transmission without ANY treatment is 25-40%; risk drops to 1% when mothers prescribed ART >4 weeks before delivery

questions.question: A woman is found to be HIV positive at 16 weeks of gestation, with a viral load of 16,000 copies/mL and CD4 count of 410.
questions.question_raw: A mother is found to be HIV+ at 16 weeks gestation. VL 16,000 copies/mL and CD4 410.

parts.text: What two recommendations should you make at the time of labour and delivery?

parts_raw.text: What 2 recommendations should you make at the time of labor and delivery?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Mode of delivery by viral load: if HIV RNA is not <1000 copies/mL near delivery, scheduled cesarean before rupture of membranes; otherwise vaginal delivery is acceptable, avoiding fetal scalp electrodes and forceps or vacuum extraction. (2) Give the newborn antiretrovirals as soon as possible, preferably within 6-12 hours of birth, and do not breastfeed.
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS perinatal guidelines: intrapartum IV zidovudine if viral load is >1000 copies/mL or unknown at delivery.

cohort_answer.text: IV zidovudine intrapartum from labor until delivery; Avoid fetal scalp monitors; C/S at 38 weeks before rupture of membranes if VL>1000 or unknown; No breastfeeding; Wash baby prior to giving IM vitamin K

questions.question: A woman co-infected with hepatitis C virus and HIV presents at 18 weeks' gestation.
questions.question_raw: HCV and HIV mom at 18 weeks

parts.text: Do you need to quantify the viral load by PCR at this point?

parts_raw.text: Need to quantify VL (PCR) at this point?

questions.model_answer: a) Yes for HIV: maternal HIV RNA drives choice of regimen, mode of delivery and neonatal antiretroviral management, and should be measured now and serially to delivery. For HCV, quantify HCV RNA (with ALT) once at entry to prenatal care to confirm viremia and stratify transmission risk; serial monitoring during pregnancy is not required, and direct-acting antiviral therapy is deferred until after pregnancy.
questions.beyond_mandell: HCV component beyond this chapter; AASLD/IDSA HCV guidance on testing in pregnancy. HIV viral-load-driven management is consistent with Mandell ch. 127.

cohort_answer.text: Yes for HIV – need to know VL. For HCV – quantify at beginning of pre-natal care (also ALT), but not during it. Vertical transmission generally confined to women with detectable HCV RNA during pregnancy. HCV RNA levels rise during 1st and 3rd trimesters, peak in 3rd trimester, decrease postpartum. Try to treat HCV before pregnancy, avoid treating during pregnancy (drugs not tested in pregnancy)

questions.question: A woman co-infected with hepatitis C virus and HIV presents at 18 weeks' gestation.
questions.question_raw: HCV and HIV mom at 18 weeks

parts.text: Is it safe to breastfeed?

parts_raw.text: Is it safe to breastfeed?

questions.model_answer: a) No, because of HIV. In the United States, Canada and other resource-rich settings breastfeeding is contraindicated for women with HIV (except in extraordinary circumstances) since breastfed infants have a clearly higher infection rate even with maternal and infant antiretrovirals. HCV alone would not contraindicate breastfeeding (avoid if nipples are cracked or bleeding), but the HIV co-infection settles the answer.
questions.beyond_mandell: HCV-and-breastfeeding statement is from CDC/AASLD guidance, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: HIV – not safe. Hep C – available evidence suggests breastfeeding by an HCV-infected mother does not appreciably increase the risk of transmitting HCV

questions.question: An HIV-infected woman is in her second pregnancy and is not on antiretroviral therapy; in her first pregnancy she took antiretrovirals which were stopped postpartum. She is now in the second trimester with a CD4 count of 450.
questions.question_raw: HIV infected woman with second pregnancy. Not on HAART. Previous pregnancy bridged with HAART stopped postpartum. What to do now (2nd trimester)? CD4 450

parts.text: What is the recommended regimen?
Why can you not use nelfinavir?
Which drugs are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy?

parts_raw.text: Recommended regimen
Why can you not use nelfinavir
Which drugs are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy?

questions.model_answer:
a) Start lifelong combination antiretroviral therapy now (do not stop postpartum), guided by resistance testing: an integrase inhibitor (dolutegravir, or raltegravir) or a boosted protease inhibitor (darunavir/r or atazanavir/r) plus a two-NRTI backbone of tenofovir/emtricitabine, tenofovir/lamivudine or abacavir/lamivudine. Aim for an undetectable viral load by delivery; add intrapartum IV zidovudine and consider caesarean section if the viral load is not <1000 copies/mL, and give the newborn antiretrovirals within 6-12 hours of birth.
b) Nelfinavir achieves low and variable plasma concentrations in pregnancy (especially the third trimester) with inferior virologic suppression; it is not teratogenic but is no longer a recommended agent.
c) Avoid didanosine plus stavudine (fatal lactic acidosis) and stavudine generally; cobicistat-boosted regimens (elvitegravir/cobicistat, darunavir/cobicistat) are not recommended because of inadequate drug levels in the second and third trimesters; efavirenz has historically been controversial early in pregnancy but is now considered acceptable.
questions.beyond_mandell: Regimen selection and drugs to avoid come from the DHHS Perinatal HIV guidelines; Mandell ch. 127 refers the reader to ch. 126 for maternal ART.

cohort_answer.text: A) RAL or DRV/r or ATZ/r or DTG + ABC/3TC or TDF/3TC or TDF/FTC. B) Nelfinavir is a PI that should NOT be used in pregnancy due to low viral suppression. C) EVG/c combinations (low ARV levels during T2/T3); EFV controversial; DDI; D4T.

questions.question: An HIV-positive woman is in her second pregnancy and is not on antiretroviral therapy; her previous pregnancy was bridged with therapy that was stopped postpartum. She is now in the second trimester with a CD4 count of 450.
questions.question_raw: HIV+ woman with second pregnancy, not on HAART, previous pregnancy bridged with HAART stopped post-partum. What to do now (2nd trimester)? CD4 450

parts.text: Why can you not use nelfinavir?

parts_raw.text: Why can you not use nelfinavir?

questions.model_answer: a) Because nelfinavir gives low, unreliable drug concentrations in pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester and postpartum, with correspondingly poor viral suppression; it is not teratogenic, but it is inadequate for preventing mother-to-child transmission.
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS Perinatal HIV guidelines (nelfinavir is a not-recommended agent in pregnancy).

cohort_answer.text: Low drug concentrations in pregnancy, especially during the 3rd trimester and post-partum. Not shown to be teratogenic

questions.question: You are consulted about a newborn whose mother was found to be HIV positive at delivery, after the baby has been delivered.
questions.question_raw: HIV in newborn. You are consulted for a woman who was found to be HIV+ during delivery (already delivered).

parts.text: How would you care for the baby?

parts_raw.text: A) How would you care for the baby?

questions.model_answer: a) This is presumed newborn HIV exposure with a mother who tested positive at delivery, so the infant is in the high-risk category. (1) No breastfeeding: formula feed, as breastfeeding is contraindicated in resource-rich settings. (2) Start antiretrovirals as soon as possible, preferably within 6-12 hours of life: empirical HIV therapy with six weeks of zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine (nevirapine at prophylactic dose) or zidovudine + lamivudine + raltegravir; some experts use combination prophylaxis (six weeks of zidovudine plus three nevirapine doses at birth, 48 hours, and 96 hours after the second dose). (3) Diagnostic testing with HIV nucleic acid tests, since maternal antibody makes serology uninterpretable before 18 months: NAT at birth/first 48 hours, then at 14-21 days, 1-2 months and 4-6 months, with an extra NAT 2-4 weeks after antiretrovirals stop (8-10 weeks of age). Any positive NAT is presumptive infection and must be confirmed immediately on a second specimen or by a different assay. (4) Baseline and monitoring bloodwork (CBC with differential, liver enzymes, creatinine) for zidovudine toxicity; co-manage with a paediatric HIV specialist. (5) Routine newborn care otherwise: standard precautions, bathing, vitamin K and ophthalmia neonatorum prophylaxis once stable. (6) Screen mother and infant for co-infections (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis) and test the mother's other children for HIV regardless of age.

cohort_answer.text: No breastfeeding; Start baby on Zidovudine + Nevirapine + Lamivudine; Check HIV PCR at delivery and in 6 weeks; CBC+Diff, ALT, Cr, lactate; Hep B, C, syphilis serologies. HIV-1 PCR and serology within 48 hours of birth; additional PCR assays at 1 month or later; HIV serology at 18-24 months to document loss of transplacental maternal antibody

questions.question: An HIV-positive mother with no antenatal care presents at delivery.
questions.question_raw: HIV in the neonate: HIV+ mom presents at delivery with no antenatal care

parts.text: What is the baby's risk of acquiring HIV?
List four (or seven) factors that increase the risk.
The baby tests HIV positive by PCR. Now what?
What is the treatment of neonatal HIV?

parts_raw.text: A) What is baby's risk of acquiring HIV?
B) List 4 (or 7) factors that increase risk
D) Baby tests HIV+ by PCR. Now what?
E) Treatment of Neonatal HIV

questions.model_answer:
a) Without any antiretrovirals in pregnancy or intrapartum, mother-to-child transmission is roughly 13-39% (about 25% overall); in the absence of therapy about 50% of transmission occurs at labour and delivery, 25% antenatally and 25% postnatally through breastfeeding. Intrapartum and neonatal antiretrovirals reduce this substantially (the US rate fell from 25% to 8% with the zidovudine regimen and is now under 2%).
b) (1) Late initiation or complete absence of combination antiretroviral therapy in pregnancy. (2) Maternal HIV RNA above 1000 copies/mL. (3) Low maternal CD4 count. (4) Prolonged rupture of membranes. (5) Preterm delivery. (6) Concomitant genital ulcerative disease. (7) Seroconversion/acute HIV infection during pregnancy or breastfeeding. (Also vaginal delivery without suppression, and breastfeeding.)
c) A positive nucleic acid test is presumptive infection only: repeat immediately on a separate blood draw, or use the alternative assay (RNA if DNA PCR was used, or vice versa) on the original sample, to confirm. Once confirmed, switch from prophylaxis/empirical therapy to full three-drug HIV treatment at treatment doses, refer to a paediatric HIV specialist, and plan lifelong therapy; serology at 15-18 months is not needed for diagnosis but maternal antibody persists to that age.
d) Combination antiretroviral therapy at treatment doses: zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine, or zidovudine + lamivudine + raltegravir, started as early as possible and continued lifelong, with Pneumocystis prophylaxis and monitoring of blood counts, liver enzymes and renal function.
questions.beyond_mandell: Pneumocystis prophylaxis and the childhood immunization details in the cohort answer are covered elsewhere, not in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text:
25% (in absence of ARV), reported rates 13-42%. With ARVs in labour, risk up to 10%
No ARV during pregnancy; Primary HIV infection (high viral load at seroconversion); High viral load >1000 at delivery; Low maternal CD4 count; Vaginal delivery; No intrapartum ARVs; Preterm delivery; Mom concurrent infections; STI; Chorioamnionitis
Repeat HIV PCR at 2 weeks to confirm; need 2 positive specimens from different draws to confirm; refer to pediatric HIV specialist; lifelong ARVs; check HIV antibody at 18 months
Zidovudine + Nevirapine + Lamivudine; Septra for 1st year of life; bloodwork monitoring (CBC, Cr, LFTs); vaccines (Hep B, meningococcal, pneumococcal, HiB, pneumococcal after 24 months, rotavirus if not severely immunocompromised, HPV/TDAP/MMR if CD4>200)

questions.question: A patient with HIV is pregnant and is not on treatment.
questions.question_raw: A patient with HIV is pregnant. She is not on treatment:

parts.text: Name three antiretroviral regimens, and when would you start them?
What two recommendations do you have for the mother at delivery?
What regimen for the baby, and timing?
When would you test the baby?
Two current Canadian recommendations for feeding?

parts_raw.text: Name 3 antiretroviral regimens and when would you start them?
b. What 2 recommendations do you have for the mother at delivery?
c. What regimen for the baby and timing?
d. When would you test the baby?
e. 2 current Canadian recommendations for feeding?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Dolutegravir + abacavir/lamivudine (HLA-B*5701 negative only). (2) Dolutegravir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)/emtricitabine. (3) Ritonavir-boosted darunavir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)/emtricitabine. Start as soon as possible — pregnancy favours immediate initiation and earlier suppression means lower transmission risk.
b) (1) If the viral load is >1000 copies/mL, scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks with intrapartum IV zidovudine; if suppressed, vaginal delivery is acceptable. (2) Avoid invasive procedures — artificial rupture of membranes, fetal scalp electrodes, forceps or vacuum.
c) Start within 6 hours of birth: zidovudine alone for 4 weeks if the mother was suppressed on ART; presumptive three-drug therapy (zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine or raltegravir) if the mother was untreated or not suppressed.
d) HIV nucleic acid (DNA/RNA) testing — at birth (high-risk), 14–21 days, 1–2 months, and 4–6 months, with confirmatory testing of any positive result; antibody testing is not diagnostic in infancy because of transplacental maternal antibody.
e) (1) Exclusive formula (replacement) feeding is recommended in Canada, where safe replacement feeding is available. (2) Avoid mixed feeding; if a virally suppressed mother chooses to breastfeed after counselling, support her with exclusive breastfeeding, maintained maternal suppression, and close infant monitoring.
questions.beyond_mandell: Infant prophylaxis, diagnostic testing schedule and CPS/DHHS infant-feeding guidance are from the DHHS Perinatal guidelines and the Canadian Paediatric Society statement; not in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: a) Dolutegravir/Abacavir/Lamivudine; TAF/Emtricitabine plus dolutegravir (or TDF); TAF/Emtricitabine plus Darunavir/ritonavir (or TDF, better studied). Start ASAP. b) VL>1000: C-section at 38 weeks and intrapartum zidovudine. VL<1000: delivery mode determined by OB, consider intrapartum zidovudine. Avoid artificial rupture of membranes, forceps/vacuum extractor, fetal scalp electrodes. c) Presumptive therapy at birth with Zidovudine, lamivudine + nevirapine or raltegravir. d) HIV NAT at birth and 6 weeks. e) Exclusive formula; no mixed feeding (solid/liquid foods prior to 6 months increases HIV transmission risk).

questions.model_answer: a) Early syphilis, non-primary non-secondary (early latent): asymptomatic with documented seroconversion within the previous 12 months. b) Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose; this is the recommended regimen for early syphilis regardless of HIV status. c) Doxycycline 100 mg PO bid for 14 days (or tetracycline 500 mg PO qid for 14 days); ceftriaxone 1-2 g IM/IV daily for 10-14 days is an alternative - azithromycin is not recommended in this setting.

cohort_answer.text: Stage: Early latent - asymptomatic with a negative test within 1 year (if no negative test within last year, automatically late latent). Treatment: 1x dose benzathine penicillin 2.4M units, given as 2x1.2M unit doses IM to each buttock. Alternatives: Doxy 100mg PO BID 10-14 days, ceftriaxone 1g IV/IM daily 10-14 days

questions.question: An infant was born one hour ago to a mother without antenatal care who was diagnosed with HIV and HBV during delivery. What can now be done for the newborn to reduce HIV and HBV transmission (give two for each)?
questions.question_raw: Infant just born one hour ago to a mother without antenatal care who was diagnosed with HIV and HBV during delivery

parts.text: Now what can be done for the newborn to reduce HIV and HBV transmission (need two for each)

parts_raw.text: Now what can be done for newborn to reduce HIV and HBV transmission (need two for each)

questions.model_answer: HIV: (1) Start infant antiretroviral prophylaxis promptly (presumptive combination therapy, e.g. zidovudine-based multidrug regimen). (2) Avoid breastfeeding (formula feed) and perform early HIV virologic (PCR) testing. HBV: (1) Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth. (2) Give hepatitis B vaccine now, with further doses at 1 and 6 months.
questions.beyond_mandell: Neonatal HIV prophylaxis and no-breastfeeding recommendations are from perinatal HIV (DHHS/PHAC) guidelines, not this chapter; the HBV HBIG + vaccine schedule is Mandell p. 1959.

cohort_answer.text: HIV: No breastfeeding; Start triple therapy ZDV+NVP+3TC (ZDV 6 weeks, 3 doses NVP first week +/-3TC); HIV test at 6 weeks. HBV: Give HBIg within 12 hours of birth; give HBV vaccine now, at 1 month and 6 months

questions.question: A woman co-infected with hepatitis C virus and HIV presents at 18 weeks' gestation.
questions.question_raw: HCV and HIV mom at 18 weeks

parts.text: What is the risk of vertical transmission of hepatitis C virus?

parts_raw.text: Risk of transmission of HCV?

questions.model_answer: a) Approximately 5-6% (pooled ~5.8%) from HCV-viremic mothers without HIV, rising to roughly 10-11% with HIV co-infection, particularly if the HIV is not virologically suppressed. Transmission is essentially confined to women with detectable HCV RNA.
questions.beyond_mandell: Not in this chapter (Mandell ch. 127 covers HIV MTCT only); figures from AASLD/IDSA HCV guidance and systematic-review data on HCV vertical transmission.

cohort_answer.text: Recent systematic review demonstrated a vertical transmission rate of 5.8% (95% CI 4.2-7.8) from HCV-infected mothers without HIV co-infection, and 10.8% (95% CI 7.6-15.2) with sub-optimally controlled HIV co-infection. ~10% in mothers with HIV and Hep C co-infection; 5-6% in mothers with Hep C mono-infection

questions.question: A woman with no antenatal care presents in labour and tests positive for HIV and hepatitis B on rapid testing.
questions.question_raw: Woman with no antenatal care presents in labor, tests positive for HIV and Hepatitis B on rapid testing.

parts.text: Give two strategies to decrease the risk of hepatitis B virus transmission to the baby.

parts_raw.text: 2 strategies to decrease risk of HBV transmission to baby

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Give the infant hepatitis B immune globulin plus the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth, completing the vaccine series on schedule. (2) Start maternal antiviral therapy active against HBV (tenofovir), which can be built into the mother's antiretroviral regimen given the HIV co-infection, to lower maternal HBV DNA.
questions.beyond_mandell: HBV perinatal prophylaxis is outside Mandell ch. 127; AASLD hepatitis B guidance and CDC/ACIP perinatal HBV recommendations.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer lists HIV-transmission measures (IV zidovudine, elective caesarean, avoiding breastfeeding and scalp electrodes) rather than the HBV-specific interventions the part asks for.

cohort_answer.text: IV zidovudine during labor until delivery; Elective CS recommended before rupture of membranes if VL unknown; Measure mom's VL and resistance testing; Avoid breastfeeding; Avoid fetal scalp monitoring
